headline: High-risk shared-filesystem and code-execution pairing: Open Interpreter can read/write local files while LightAgent can ingest and emit MCP/tool content, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: LightAgent can use MCP and processes tool results, while Open Interpreter can read the filesystem, use the clipboard, and execute shell commands. That creates a plausible bridge where attacker-controlled content from one agent can be consumed by the other as instructions. The pair lacks documented provenance isolation, so uncertainty pushes this above low.
conditions: IF Open Interpreter reads LightAgent-generated files or clipboard text as instructions, injection is possible.
IF the pair shares a filesystem or clipboard bridge, attacker-controlled content can cross agents.
mitigations: Disable clipboard-based handoff between agents.
Use separate working directories with read-only sharing.
Add provenance tags to all inter-agent files.
Require manual review of any text that becomes a prompt.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitizing wrappers around MCP/file inputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: LightAgent touches user conversations, long-term memory, tool results, and secrets, and Open Interpreter can read the entire local filesystem and has broad network egress. If LightAgent outputs are written to shared files or copied via clipboard, Open Interpreter can exfiltrate sensitive data to external services. The default overlap is dangerous and the blast radius includes secrets and local data.
conditions: IF LightAgent writes conversations, memory, or tool results into a shared directory, Open Interpreter can read them.
IF Open Interpreter forwards those contents to a model provider or other network endpoint, leakage occurs.
mitigations: Keep agents on separate user accounts.
Store LightAgent outputs in a private directory not mounted into Open Interpreter.
Turn off clipboard transfer for sensitive material.
Restrict Open Interpreter network access during shared workflows.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: LightAgent can spawn subprocesses and use MCP, while Open Interpreter can execute shell commands, modify git state, write the filesystem, and install packages. Both support multiple instances, and Open Interpreter shares state via filesystem, so concurrent writes to the same workspace can corrupt files or git history. This is a direct overlapping-write conflict in default-capable setups.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory, file races can occur.
IF both modify the same git repository without locking, history corruption or lost work can occur.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate workspace.
Use file locks around shared artifacts.
Disable git writes for one agent during coordination.
Run one agent at a time for mutable tasks.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: LightAgent produces tool results, workflow state, and provenance metadata, while Open Interpreter can act on local files and execute shell commands. If Open Interpreter treats LightAgent output as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into destructive local actions or commits. Because Open Interpreter has action-taking authority, the downstream blast radius is high.
conditions: IF Open Interpreter consumes LightAgent output without verification, incorrect facts can trigger actions.
IF LightAgent emits malformed provenance metadata, Open Interpreter may propagate it into files or commits.
mitigations: Require human approval before shell or git actions.
Validate LightAgent outputs against a schema.
Separate planning from execution roles.
Log and diff all proposed actions before execution.
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking gates.

E_compliance.rationale: LightAgent handles user conversations, long-term memory, and secrets, while Open Interpreter can access anything reachable on the local machine and has broad network egress. If regulated data is present on the host, the pair can move it into a less controlled environment or across residency boundaries. The profiles do not specify certifications or residency controls, so uncertainty escalates to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF regulated data is present in LightAgent memory or local files, Open Interpreter can access it.
IF Open Interpreter sends that data to external model providers, residency or retention obligations may be violated.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared workspaces.
Use a local-only model provider for Open Interpreter.
Purge sensitive memory before handoff.
Document retention and deletion responsibilities.
requires-engineering: add residency-aware routing and audit logs.
